title: "1. Design the Scenes"
description: "Break the explanation into scenes with purpose, location, characters, and learning outcome. Produce scenes.md."

## Overview

With characters cast and a metaphor mapped, you need a plan for *how the story
unfolds*. A scene is the unit the listener experiences and the unit the producer
renders. Each scene must have a purpose, a location, participating characters,
and — most importantly — an **educational outcome**: what should the learner
understand after hearing it?

This lesson teaches scene design through a narrative arc, then shows you how to
write a `scenes.md` file.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Explain why technical storytelling needs a narrative arc, not documentation
  read aloud.
- Describe the eight-beat arc structure: Introduction, Question, Discovery,
  Increasing complexity, Challenge, Climax, Resolution, Technical takeaway.
- Write a `scenes.md` file where every scene specifies: Goal, Technical concept,
  Location, Characters, Action, Sound, Transition, Learning outcome.
- Ensure every scene answers: *What did I learn about the technical model from
  this scene?*

## The narrative arc

Technical storytelling is not documentation read aloud. It needs a lightweight
dramatic structure that guides the listener from curiosity to understanding:

```
Introduction         A seemingly simple request.
       |
Question / Problem   How does that request become a working system?
       |
Discovery            The first components of the system appear.
       |
Increasing complexity The system grows: more parts, more relationships.
       |
Challenge            Something must be verified, checked, or reconciled.
       |
Climax               The abstraction proves its value — why it all works.
       |
Resolution           The metaphor reconnects to the real technology.
       |
Technical takeaway   The one thing the listener should remember.
```

Each beat in the arc becomes one or more scenes. You do not need to hit every
beat in every story, but the arc gives you a skeleton to hang your scenes on.

::: {.callout-tip}
The climax is where the *abstraction pays off*. For Crossplane, the climax is
the realization that one request becomes many components without the developer
ever talking to providers. For your own system, ask: *what is the moment where
the design decision proves its worth?*
:::

## What goes into a scene

Every scene in `scenes.md` must specify:

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Goal | What the scene accomplishes in the story. |
| Technical concept | Which part of the technical model it explains. |
| Location | Where the scene takes place in the metaphor world. |
| Characters | Who participates. |
| Action | What happens — the dramatic event. |
| Sound | Key sound effects or ambience that mark events. |
| Transition | How the scene ends and leads into the next. |
| Learning outcome | What the learner should understand afterward. |

## Modeling on the reference example

The Crossplane restaurant traces the arc like this:

| Beat | Scene | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Introduction | 01 — The Front of House | Customer arrives, makes a request. |
| Question | 02 — Order Placed | How does a request become a concrete order? |
| Discovery | 03 — The Kitchen | The recipe (Composition) is matched to the order. |
| Increasing complexity | 04 — Preparing the Components | Many managed resources are composed. |
| Increasing complexity | 05 — The Kitchen Capability | Providers realize components in the real world. |
| Challenge | 06 — Perfecting the Dish | Reconciliation checks and corrects. |
| Climax / Resolution | 07 — Served and Connected | The abstraction lands; metaphor reconnects to Crossplane. |

Read the full scene plan at
[`reference-example/scenes.md`](../../reference-example/scenes.md).

## Writing your scenes.md

For each scene, write a short block like:

```
### SCENE 01 — [TITLE]
- **Goal:** [what this scene accomplishes]
- **Technical concept:** [which concept from concept.md]
- **Location:** [metaphor-world setting]
- **Characters:** [who participates]
- **Action:** [dramatic event]
- **Sound:** [key SFX / ambience]
- **Transition:** [how it ends]
- **Learning outcome:** [what the learner takes away]
```

After writing all scenes, read through them and ask: *can the learner explain
the technical model just from these outcomes?* If a concept is missing, add a
scene or adjust an existing one.
